newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian insurgents defy army in border region.
newsitem.headline: Albanian insurgents defy army in border region.

text.p: The Albanian army, in its first clash with insurgents near the Greek border, retreated with a bloody nose on Wednesday but kept a heavy presence in the volatile southern region.

Eyewitnesses said four insurgents and at least two soldiers were wounded in the fighting about 10 kms (six miles) inland from this port town. Hospital officials said one of the wounded rebels was in a serious condition.
A state of emergency has been in effect since Sunday and one wounded insurgent told reporters the army had operated under the shoot-on-sight order which went into effect on Monday.
Rebels in Sarande staged of boisterous rally in the main square in the evening, defying a nightly curfew, and holding guns and babies aloft while chanting anti-government slogans.

Army tanks and armoured personnel carriers (APCs) roamed the roads to the east near the main regional town of Gjirokaster, 30 kms (18 miles) north of the border, a Reuters correspondent in the area reported.
Sporadic bursts from assault rifles were heard throughout the day in Sarande, a main bastion of the defiant rebels who are challenging the rule of President Sali Berisha.
Early in the day, dozens of soldiers were deployed between Sarande and Delvine, 20 kms (12 miles) to the east, in the first major clash between the regular army and the insurgents.
After a brief fight, the insurgents claimed a victory when the soldiers retreated.

"Fighting lasted about 40 minutes and at least two soldiers were wounded. The people won. The army, about 60 soldiers, got in their trucks and left," Dimitris Stefos, the former prefect in Sarande, told Reuters by telephone.

Albania has been swept by anti-government protests and riots since January, when five popular pyramid investment schemes collapsed. Many Albanian families lost money in the fraudulent schemes, in which the equivalent of $1 billion to $2 billion in savings disappeared overnight.
Protests over the schemes have become a direct challenge to Berisha, especially in the relatively better-off southern region stretching from Vlore to Sarande.

Berisha was elected president by parliament in 1992 after his Democrats won the popular vote in the first free election after the fall of 45 years of Stalinist rule. He was re-elected to a new five-year term this week.
But anger over the failed pyramid schemes has spread across the country and at the weekend rioters burned and looted in the border region. They stole thousands of arms from state arsenals.
Security force fled, leaving the masked and armed insurgents to roam the streets with impunity.
During the fighting on Wednesday, an Albanian fighter aircraft swooped over the battlefield and three columns of thick smoke could be seen rising from a nearby hillside.
It was unclear whether the Russian-designed MiG fighter had bombed the village or been shot down -- as claimed by insurgents leaving the area.

Near Sarande, armed gangs seized an army tank from its crew and drove it gleefully through the streets. About a dozen tanks had taken up positions at key junctions during the night but had let traffic pass normally.
Gangs of gunmen drove around town in large, open trucks and one group went joyriding in a white van with the letters of the United Nations written on the side.

A Reuters photographer said several hundred heavily armed rebels had set up a defence line on a hillside at the entrance to Sarande. The rebels said they were determined to take on the army whatever the cost.
"Neither Berisha nor the army will pass us without a fight to the finish," a rebel on the hilltop told the photographer.

Anti-government riots swept southern Albania at the weekend and rioters seized an array of weapons from state arsenals. They looted stores and burned down warehouses throughout the region, where there is a large ethnic Greek minority.
Between 300 and400 local rebels at the entrance to Sarande brandished assault rifles and rocket-propelled grenades. They had dug in with anti-aircraft guns and heavy machineguns.
"People's justice" was dished out in Sarande to suspected secret police and Greek television footage showed a man tied to a telephone pole and being kicked repeatedly in the face.
